questions.title: Transposons: mobile DNA and toxin genes
questions.question: Transposons?

options.B: Carry genes that code for toxin production
options.D: Mobile DNA sequence that can move from one site to another site.

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. Transposons are DNA elements, not RNA-containing genetic elements, so this statement alone is false and not part of the correct combined answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone (true but partial). Transposons can indeed carry genes that code for toxin production, but this is only one of two jointly true statements the key combines, not the complete answer by itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transposons, unlike plasmids, do not replicate autonomously -- they depend on being part of a replicon (the chromosome or a plasmid) to be copied, which is exactly why this statement is excluded from the combined correct answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect alone (true but partial). A transposon is indeed a mobile DNA sequence that can move from one site to another (popularly called a "jumping gene"), but this is only one of two jointly true statements the key combines, not the complete answer alone.
explanations.E: Correct. Transposons are best described by combining two of the listed statements: they are mobile DNA sequences able to move from one site to another (B, the defining "jumping gene" property) and they can carry genes that code for toxin production (D) -- while they do not contain RNA and, unlike plasmids, do not replicate autonomously. Since two separate listed statements are both true and the others are not, "B & D" is the correct composite answer rather than any single option alone.

questions.learning_objective: State that transposons are mobile DNA sequences that can carry toxin genes, while not containing RNA and not replicating autonomously.

questions.title: Transposons: the false statement
questions.question: The following statements are correct regarding transposons EXCEPT?

options.A: Can carry genes that code for antibiotic resistance
options.B: Can move from plasmid to another

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement, so not the EXCEPT answer). Transposons can indeed carry genes that code for antibiotic resistance, one of the classic ways resistance genes spread between replicons.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). Transposons can indeed move from one plasmid to another (or between a plasmid and the chromosome), which is exactly their "jumping gene" mobility.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement). Transposons are transmissible in the sense that they can move between DNA molecules and be carried along when their host replicon (a plasmid, for instance) is transferred.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Transposons do not autonomously replicate -- unlike a plasmid, a transposon has no independent origin of replication of its own and depends entirely on being part of a chromosome or plasmid to be copied along with that larger replicon.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that transposons do not autonomously replicate, while correctly carrying resistance genes, moving between plasmids, and being transmissible.

questions.title: R plasmids: antibiotic resistance genes
questions.question: Plasmids which carry Antibiotic resistance genes are called?

explanations.A: Incorrect. F plasmids (fertility factors) carry genes for sex pilus formation and conjugative transfer, not specifically antibiotic-resistance genes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bacteriocins are antibacterial proteins some bacteria produce, not a category of plasmid at all.
explanations.C: Correct. Plasmids that carry genes for bacterial antibiotic resistance are called R plasmids (resistance plasmids). This resistance-gene cargo is the R plasmid's defining feature, and such plasmids are frequently also conjugative, allowing resistance genes to spread rapidly through a bacterial population.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Ori plasmid" is not standard terminology for a resistance-carrying plasmid; "ori" more generally refers to an origin of replication, a feature every plasmid has, not a resistance-specific category.

questions.learning_objective: Identify R plasmids as the plasmid category that carries antibiotic-resistance genes, distinguishing them from F plasmids, bacteriocins, and "ori plasmids."

questions.title: F plasmids: sex pilus formation genes
questions.question: Plasmids which carry genes for sex pilus formation are called?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Episome" describes a plasmid's ability to integrate into the host chromosome, a different property from carrying sex-pilus genes specifically.
explanations.B: Correct. Plasmids that carry the genes for sex pilus formation are called F plasmids (fertility factors) -- the sex pilus they encode is what establishes cell-to-cell contact and mediates conjugative DNA transfer. This sex-pilus-gene cargo, together with the conjugation ability it confers, is the F plasmid's defining feature.
explanations.C: Incorrect. R plasmids are defined by carrying antibiotic-resistance genes, not specifically by carrying sex-pilus-formation genes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Col factors are plasmids carrying genes for bacteriocin (colicin) production, an antibacterial protein, not sex-pilus formation genes.

questions.learning_objective: Identify F plasmids as the plasmid category that carries genes for sex pilus formation, distinguishing them from episomes, R plasmids, and Col factors.

questions.title: Fertility factor mediates gene transfer by conjugation
questions.question: Fertility Factor can mediate gene transfer by?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Transformation is uptake of free naked DNA by a competent recipient; it does not require, or involve, the fertility factor.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Transduction is mediated by a bacteriophage, not by the fertility factor.
explanations.C: Correct. The fertility factor (F plasmid) mediates gene transfer specifically by conjugation: it encodes the sex pilus that establishes cell-to-cell contact and the transfer machinery that moves DNA (including itself) from a donor to a recipient cell. This F-plasmid-to-conjugation link is exactly why cells carrying an F plasmid are called F+ (donor-capable), unlike F- cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Transposition is an intracellular movement of a transposon between DNA sites; it does not describe cell-to-cell gene transfer mediated by the fertility factor.

questions.learning_objective: State that the fertility factor mediates gene transfer by conjugation, distinguishing it from transformation, transduction and transposition.

questions.title: Transposons: mobile gene sequences
questions.question: Mobile sequences of genes that can move into different sites in the microbial DNA?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A plasmid is a whole, independently replicating extrachromosomal DNA molecule; it does not itself "move into different sites" the way a transposon does within a larger DNA molecule.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The chromosome is the cell's own large, essential DNA molecule -- the structure a transposon moves within, not itself a mobile element.
explanations.C: Correct. Transposons are, by definition, mobile sequences of genes that can move from one site to another within or between DNA molecules in the microbial genome. They are popularly called "jumping genes" for exactly this reason. This site-to-site mobility is the defining property of a transposon, distinguishing it from a whole replicon such as a plasmid, chromosome, or episome.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An episome is a plasmid capable of integrating into the host chromosome as a whole unit; it is not itself the small, internally mobile gene sequence a transposon is.

questions.learning_objective: Identify transposons as mobile gene sequences that move between sites in microbial DNA, distinguishing them from plasmids, the chromosome, and episomes.

questions.title: Helicase: breaking hydrogen bonds between nucleotides
questions.question: Enzyme which breaks the hydrogen bonds between nucleotides?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ligase seals nicks in the DNA backbone, joining fragments together (such as Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand) by forming a phosphodiester bond -- it does not break hydrogen bonds between base pairs.
explanations.B: Correct. Helicase is, by definition, the enzyme that breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary nucleotide base pairs, unwinding the DNA duplex ahead of the replication fork and producing the two separated single strands that serve as templates for new DNA synthesis. Without helicase's unwinding action, the two other replication proteins -- single-strand binding proteins, which stabilise the separated strands, and DNA polymerase, which needs single-stranded template -- would have nothing to act on.
explanations.C: Incorrect. DNA polymerase synthesizes a new DNA strand by adding nucleotides complementary to an already-single-stranded template; it does not itself break the hydrogen bonds holding the original duplex together.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Primase synthesizes the short RNA primer needed to give DNA polymerase a starting point; it does not break hydrogen bonds to unwind the duplex.

questions.learning_objective: Identify helicase as the enzyme that breaks hydrogen bonds between nucleotides to unwind DNA, distinguishing it from ligase, polymerase and primase.

questions.title: Codon: three nucleotides in the mRNA reading frame
questions.question: Each 3 nucleotides in the reading frame of mRNA are called?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A primer is a short segment that starts DNA synthesis; it is not the name for a 3-nucleotide reading-frame unit on mRNA.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A promoter is a regulatory DNA sequence upstream of a gene where RNA polymerase binds to begin transcription; it is not a 3-base unit of the mRNA reading frame.
explanations.C: Correct. Each group of 3 successive nucleotides in the reading frame of mRNA is, by definition, called a codon -- the basic code word that specifies one amino acid (or a start/stop signal) during translation. This 3-base grouping is what makes the genetic code a triplet code, read in a fixed, non-overlapping frame from the initiating codon.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An anticodon is the complementary 3-base sequence carried on a tRNA molecule that pairs with the mRNA codon; it is the tRNA's counterpart to a codon, not the codon on mRNA itself.

questions.learning_objective: Define a codon as each group of 3 nucleotides in the mRNA reading frame, distinguishing it from a primer, promoter, and anticodon.

questions.title: Restriction endonuclease: recognizing and cleaving a specific sequence
questions.question: Recognize a specific nucleotide sequence and cleave the DNA at this recognition site?

explanations.A: Incorrect. DNA polymerase synthesizes new DNA by extending an existing primer; it does not recognise a specific sequence purely in order to cleave DNA there.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Primase synthesizes the short RNA primer needed to start DNA synthesis; it does not recognise a specific sequence and cleave DNA at that site.
explanations.C: Correct. A restriction endonuclease is, by definition, a bacterial enzyme that recognises a specific (often palindromic) nucleotide sequence and cleaves the DNA at that recognition site. It is exactly this specific recognition, rather than indiscriminate cutting, that makes restriction endonucleases the basic working tool of recombinant DNA technology and molecular cloning.
explanations.D: Incorrect. DNA ligase seals nicks in the DNA backbone by joining fragments together (forming a phosphodiester bond); it repairs breaks rather than recognising a sequence to create one.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a restriction endonuclease as the enzyme that recognises a specific nucleotide sequence and cleaves DNA there, distinguishing it from DNA polymerase, primase and DNA ligase.

questions.title: Specialized transduction: transfer of specific bacterial DNA
questions.question: The transfer of specific parts of bacterial DNA to another bacterial cell can be mediated by?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Transformation transfers free naked DNA taken up from the environment; it is not restricted to transferring specific parts of bacterial DNA in the way described here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Conjugation transfers DNA through direct cell-to-cell contact, typically an entire plasmid; it is not the phage-mediated mechanism specifically restricted to genes near a prophage's integration site.
explanations.C: Correct. Specialized (restricted) transduction is, by definition, mediated by a temperate phage and transfers only the specific parts of bacterial DNA located adjacent to that phage's own integration site in the bacterial chromosome -- not DNA at random from anywhere in the genome. This restriction to a specific chromosomal neighbourhood is exactly what "specialized" names, distinguishing it from generalized transduction's random-DNA delivery by a virulent phage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Generalized transduction, mediated by a virulent (lytic) phage, transfers DNA essentially at random from anywhere in the donor genome, not specifically restricted parts near one site.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Recombination is the general process of exchanging DNA segments between molecules once they are already present in the same cell; it is not itself a mechanism of transfer between two separate bacterial cells.

questions.learning_objective: Identify specialized transduction as the mechanism, mediated by a temperate phage, that transfers specific parts of bacterial DNA to another cell.

questions.title: Conjugative plasmid features: the exception
questions.question: All the following characterize conjugative plasmids EXCEPT?

options.A: They may carry antibiotic resistance genes
options.C: Their transfer between cells does not need cell to cell contact
options.D: They can be transferred between different species and genera
options.E: The cell that receives it becomes a donor cell

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement, so not the EXCEPT answer). Conjugative plasmids frequently carry antibiotic-resistance genes, a major route by which resistance spreads.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). Conjugative plasmids carry the tra (transfer) genes that encode the sex pilus and the machinery needed to mediate their own transfer.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Conjugation, by definition, requires direct cell-to-cell contact -- a sex pilus forms a mating bridge connecting donor and recipient -- so a conjugative plasmid's transfer specifically does need cell-to-cell contact, the opposite of what this statement claims.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement). Conjugative plasmids characteristically show a wide host range and can indeed be transferred between different bacterial species and genera.
explanations.E: Incorrect (true statement). Once a recipient cell receives a conjugative plasmid, it becomes capable of acting as a donor itself, transferring that same plasmid onward to further recipients.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that conjugative plasmid transfer does require cell-to-cell contact, as the false statement among otherwise-true conjugative plasmid characters.

questions.title: Plasmids mediating conjugation: the F factor
questions.question: Plasmids that can mediate gene transfer by conjugation are known as?

explanations.A: Correct. Plasmids that can mediate gene transfer by conjugation are known as the F factor (fertility factor) -- the prototypical conjugative plasmid, encoding the sex pilus and transfer machinery that establish cell-to-cell contact and move DNA (including itself) into a recipient. "F factor" is the term specifically tied to conjugative capability, distinguishing it from plasmid categories named for other cargo (resistance, bacteriocins).
explanations.B: Incorrect. R factor (R plasmid) is defined by carrying antibiotic-resistance genes; some R plasmids are also conjugative, but the category name itself marks resistance-gene cargo, not the conjugation-mediating property being asked about here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Col factor is defined by carrying bacteriocin (colicin) genes, not by conjugative gene-transfer capability.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A conjugative transposon is a distinct mobile element that combines transposon-like mobility with conjugative transfer ability, but it is not itself the classic term this stem's answer describes (a plasmid named for its conjugation-mediating role).
explanations.E: Incorrect. A cosmid is an artificial cloning vector combining plasmid and phage-lambda features, a laboratory construct rather than a naturally occurring conjugative plasmid category.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the F factor as the plasmid category known for mediating gene transfer by conjugation, distinguishing it from R factor, Col factor, conjugative transposon and cosmid.

questions.title: Which process involves a sex pilus
questions.question: Which one of the following processes involves a sex pilus?

options.A: Conjugation resulting in transfer of an R factor
options.B: Transposition of a mobile genetic element
options.E: Recombination of a homologous genetic element

explanations.A: Correct. Conjugation is the process that specifically involves a sex pilus: the pilus establishes cell-to-cell contact and forms the mating bridge through which DNA (here, an R factor plasmid) is transferred from donor to recipient. None of the other listed processes require this structure at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Transposition is an intracellular movement of a mobile genetic element within or between DNA molecules in the same cell; it does not involve any cell-surface appendage such as a sex pilus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Integration of a temperate bacteriophage into the bacterial chromosome (establishing lysogeny) is mediated by phage-encoded recombination machinery, not by a sex pilus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Transduction delivers DNA via a bacteriophage particle injecting its contents into the cell; it does not require a sex pilus, which is specific to conjugation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Recombination between homologous DNA segments is a molecular exchange process occurring once DNA is already present in a cell; it does not itself require, or involve, a sex pilus.

questions.learning_objective: Identify conjugation as the process that involves a sex pilus, distinguishing it from transposition, phage integration, transduction and recombination.

questions.title: Transformation: susceptible to nuclease activity
questions.question: Which type of genetic exchange in bacteria is susceptible to the activity of nuclease enzymes?

explanations.A: Incorrect. During conjugation, DNA passes through a protected mating-bridge channel formed by the sex pilus, largely shielded from extracellular nucleases in the surrounding environment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. In generalized transduction the donor DNA is protected inside the bacteriophage's protein capsid during transfer, shielding it from extracellular nucleases.
explanations.C: Incorrect. In specialized transduction the donor DNA is likewise packaged and protected inside the phage particle, shielding it from extracellular nucleases.
explanations.D: Correct. Transformation is the genetic exchange type susceptible to nuclease activity, because it involves free, naked DNA released into the environment and taken up directly by a competent recipient cell -- while that DNA is extracellular and unprotected, environmental nuclease enzymes (DNases) can degrade it before uptake occurs. This exposure is exactly what distinguishes transformation's vulnerability from conjugation's and transduction's protected delivery routes.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Vertical gene transfer passes DNA from a parent cell directly to its own offspring at cell division, with no extracellular exposure of DNA to nuclease enzymes at all.

questions.learning_objective: State that transformation, unlike conjugation or transduction, is susceptible to nuclease activity because its DNA is briefly extracellular and unprotected.

questions.title: Mating pair formation: sex pilus requirement
questions.question: Formation of matting pair during the process of conjugation in E. Coli requires?

options.D: Transfer of both strands of DNA

explanations.A: Correct. Formation of a mating pair during conjugation in E. coli requires the sex pilus: it is the appendage, encoded by the F plasmid, that extends from the donor cell, makes contact with a recipient, and draws the two cells together to establish the stable mating-pair connection through which DNA is later transferred.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Restriction endonucleases recognise and cleave specific DNA sequences, a function unrelated to physically forming the mating-pair connection between two conjugating cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transposon integration is an unrelated, intracellular event involving mobile genetic elements, not the mechanism that forms a mating pair between two cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Conjugation transfers only a single strand of the plasmid DNA (with the complementary strand synthesized afterward in both donor and recipient), not both strands together as the mating-pair-forming requirement.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Common pilus" (ordinary/fimbrial pili) mediate adherence to surfaces or host cells, a different function from the sex pilus's specific role in conjugative mating-pair formation.

questions.learning_objective: State that mating pair formation during E. coli conjugation requires the sex pilus, not restriction endonuclease, transposon integration, double-stranded transfer, or common pili.

questions.title: Plasmid transmission via conjugation
questions.question: Plasmid could be transmitted to other bacteria in?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Transformation transfers free naked DNA taken up from the environment; a whole plasmid is not typically transmitted between bacteria by this route.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Generalized transduction packages random fragments of chromosomal (or occasionally plasmid) DNA inside a phage capsid; it is not the standard, primary route of plasmid transmission.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Specialized transduction transfers DNA specifically adjacent to a temperate phage's integration site in the chromosome, not the standard route by which a plasmid as a whole is transmitted.
explanations.D: Correct. A plasmid is characteristically transmitted to other bacteria by conjugation: a conjugative plasmid encodes the sex pilus and transfer machinery needed to move a copy of itself (and sometimes co-resident genes) directly into a recipient cell through cell-to-cell contact. This is the primary, most efficient mechanism by which plasmids -- and the resistance or virulence genes they often carry -- spread through a bacterial population.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Fusion" is not a recognised bacterial gene-transfer mechanism; bacteria do not transfer plasmids by cell fusion the way some eukaryotic cells might fuse.

questions.learning_objective: State that conjugation is the characteristic route by which a plasmid is transmitted to other bacteria.

questions.title: Transformation: naked DNA taken up by the recipient
questions.question: The mode of transfer in which naked DNA is directly taken by the recipient cell is known as?

explanations.A: Correct. The mode of transfer in which naked (free) DNA is taken up directly by the recipient cell is, by definition, transformation -- the recipient must be in a competent physiological state, and stable incorporation requires sequence homology with its own genome. This direct uptake of free DNA, with no phage or cell-contact intermediary, is exactly what separates transformation from transduction and conjugation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Transduction delivers DNA packaged inside a bacteriophage particle, not naked DNA taken up directly from the environment.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Conjugation transfers DNA through direct cell-to-cell contact via a sex pilus, not through direct uptake of naked extracellular DNA.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Cell transmission" is not standard terminology for any recognised bacterial gene-transfer mechanism.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Cell fusion" is not a recognised bacterial gene-transfer mechanism; bacteria do not fuse whole cells to exchange naked DNA.

questions.learning_objective: Identify transformation as the transfer mode in which naked DNA is directly taken up by the recipient cell.

questions.title: R factor: main determinant of drug resistance
questions.question: Drug resistance in bacteria is manly determined by?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The F factor is defined by mediating conjugation via the sex pilus; it is not the plasmid category specifically defined by carrying antibiotic-resistance genes.
explanations.B: Correct. Drug (antibiotic) resistance in bacteria is mainly determined by the R factor (R plasmid), the plasmid category specifically defined by carrying antibiotic-resistance genes. R factors are frequently also conjugative. This lets resistance spread rapidly through a bacterial population by the same cell-to-cell transfer mechanism that moves the F factor.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Col factors are defined by carrying bacteriocin (colicin) genes, a different cargo from antibiotic resistance.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Lysogenic factor" is not standard terminology for a plasmid category; lysogeny is a property of temperate bacteriophages, not of a resistance-determining plasmid.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Serum factor" is not a recognised bacterial genetics term; it does not name any plasmid category responsible for drug resistance.

questions.learning_objective: State that the R factor is the main determinant of drug resistance in bacteria, distinguishing it from the F factor, Col factor, and implausible distractors.

questions.title: Plasmid-governed functions: endotoxin as the exception
questions.question: Plasmid governs the following functions in bacteria EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement, so not the EXCEPT answer). Drug resistance is classically plasmid-governed (via R plasmids).
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). Various virulence factors can be plasmid-encoded, so plasmid governance of virulence is a genuine statement here.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement). Capsule production can be plasmid-governed in some bacteria, a genuine plasmid-mediated trait.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement). Bacteriocin (colicin) production is governed by Col factor plasmids, a genuine plasmid-mediated trait.
explanations.E: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide) is an intrinsic structural component of the Gram-negative cell wall, encoded by chromosomal genes -- not carried on a plasmid -- unlike drug resistance, virulence, capsule production and bacteriocin production, all of which can be plasmid-governed.

questions.learning_objective: Identify endotoxin production as chromosomally, not plasmid, encoded -- the exception among otherwise plasmid-governed bacterial functions.

questions.title: What transformation involves
questions.question: Transformation is a process of gene transfer in bacteria. It involves?

options.A: Taking up of DNA from the environment
options.B: Transfer of DNA from mother cell to its progeny
options.C: Transfer of genes between bacteria during cell contact
options.D: Transfer of genes from bacterial viruses to bacterial cell
options.E: Transfer of genes from plasmid to chromosome

explanations.A: Correct. Transformation is, by definition, the process in which a recipient bacterial cell takes up free DNA directly from the environment -- DNA that has been released there by a donor cell -- provided the recipient is in a physiologically competent state and there is sufficient sequence homology for stable incorporation. "Taking up DNA from the environment" is exactly what separates transformation from the other listed mechanisms, none of which describe uptake of free extracellular DNA.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Transfer of DNA from a mother cell to its progeny describes ordinary vertical inheritance at cell division, not transformation, which is a horizontal transfer between two existing, separate cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transfer of genes between bacteria during cell contact describes conjugation, not transformation, which specifically does not require cell-to-cell contact.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Transfer of genes from bacterial viruses to a bacterial cell describes transduction, not transformation, which does not involve a bacteriophage at all.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Transfer of genes from a plasmid to the chromosome describes an episome's integration event, not transformation, which is a mechanism of transfer between cells, not within one cell's own DNA.

questions.learning_objective: State that transformation involves taking up DNA from the environment, distinguishing it from vertical inheritance, conjugation, transduction and episome integration.

questions.title: Transduction: DNA portion transfer via bacteriophage
questions.question: The transfer of a portion of the DNA from one bacterium to another by bacteriophage is known as?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Transcription is the intracellular process of making RNA from a DNA template; it does not describe transfer of DNA between two bacteria.
explanations.B: Correct. The transfer of a portion of DNA from one bacterium to another by bacteriophage is, by definition, transduction -- the phage packages donor DNA during its replication in one bacterium and delivers it into the next bacterium it infects. This bacteriophage-mediated route is exactly what distinguishes transduction from transformation's free-DNA uptake and conjugation's direct cell contact.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Translation is the intracellular process of making protein from mRNA; it does not describe transfer of DNA between two bacteria.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Complementation is a genetic test in which two mutant alleles, present together, restore a normal phenotype; it is not itself a mechanism of transferring DNA between bacteria.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Conjugation transfers DNA through direct cell-to-cell contact via a sex pilus, not by means of a bacteriophage.

questions.learning_objective: Identify transduction as the transfer of a portion of DNA from one bacterium to another by bacteriophage, distinguishing it from transcription, translation, complementation and conjugation.
